title: Adaptive microbatch slicing and token-priority protocol
content:
Summary:
This note sketches a lightweight, implementable protocol for coordinating prefetch (what we usually call 'prefill') and decode pipelines via adaptive microbatch slicing and per-token priority scoring. Goal: reduce median and tail latency for interactive streams while preserving throughput on large concurrent workloads and minimizing KV cache churn.

Motivation and high-level goals:
- Observed problem: large prefill microbatches reduce per-token cost but increase tail latency for short/interactive streams. Conversely, tiny microbatches hurt throughput and increase kernel overhead.
- Hypothesis: dynamically slicing microbatches based on a token-priority score and using a credit-style handshake between prefetch and decode threads can get the best of both worlds.
- Secondary goal: limit KV cache residency churn by biasing slices to reuse hot KV entries and by introducing small grace windows for eviction.

Core ideas (overview):
1) Token-priority score (TPS): every incoming request is scored at admission using simple features: stream SLA class (S0..S3), estimated response length, recent per-stream latency record, and whether the request can reuse a hot KV key (boolean). TPS is an integer 0..100.
2) Microbatch slices: instead of forming a single static microbatch per cycle, we form 2..N slices per kernel timeslice. Slices are ordered by TPS windows (e.g., high-priority: TPS>=70, mid: 40..69, low:<40).
3) Credit handshake: each decode worker advertises how many tokens it can accept in the next timeslice (credits). Prefill allocates slices to decoders based on credits and priority windows. Prefetch will not overcommit KV entries if decode credits are zero (no-op).
4) Adaptive slice sizing: slice size is a function of current global load, latency tail metric, and observed kernel throughput. When kernels are idle and tail high, prefer smaller slices and more priority interleaving. When throughput is saturated but tails low, grow slices to increase amortization.
5) KV residency grace windows: when a KV key is loaded for a given model/seq-length bucket, mark it hot for G milliseconds (configurable). Prefetch will attempt to schedule new slices that reuse hot keys across adjacent slices within the same grace window. This reduces re-loads and memory traffic.

Admission and scoring details:
- Admission step attaches metadata to each request: client_sla, estimated_max_tokens (prompt+expected gen), affinity_key (if present), request_age.
- TPS = base_by_SLA + len_penalty + locality_boost + recency_boost
  - base_by_SLA: S0=60, S1=40, S2=20, S3=0 (values tunable)
  - len_penalty: -min(estimated_max_tokens/2, 20)
  - locality_boost: +20 if affinity_key maps to a hot KV key currently resident on target node
  - recency_boost: +10 if this stream had a recent latency violation (within 1s)
- Cap TPS to [0,100]. Map TPS to one of three slice buckets: high(70-100), mid(40-69), low(0-39).

Slice formation and scheduling algorithm (pseudocode):
1. Collector maintains per-priority ring buffers: highQ, midQ, lowQ. Incoming requests are appended to appropriate queue.
2. Every kernel_timeslice (configurable, e.g., 4ms) scheduler polls decoder credits and forms slices:
   - available_credits = sum(decoder.credit for decoder in live_decoders)
   - target_total_tokens = clamp(available_credits * target_utilization, min_tokens, max_tokens)
   - For each priority in [high, mid, low]: allocate tokens proportional to weight (weights configurable, default: high=0.5, mid=0.3, low=0.2).
   - For each queue: pop requests until allocated tokens exhausted or queue empty. Create a slice object {requests[], total_tokens, affinity_keys[]}. Mark slice.hint_hot_keys = union of affinity_keys present.
   - For slices that share hint_hot_keys and are scheduled within same grace window, prefer co-placement on same device/slot.

Credit handshake and backpressure:
- Decoder state: {available_credits, current_kernel_busy_until}
- Prefetch handshake: before emitting a slice with KV load operations, prefetch must verify target_decoder.available_credits >= slice.total_tokens. If not satisfied, either:
  1) shrink slice by removing low TPS requests, or
  2) move slice to the head of the same priority queue and attempt next timeslice.
- If a decoder detects imminent KV eviction pressure (memory over threshold), it can broadcast a soft_no_load signal; prefetch will then only emit slices whose keys are already resident. Hard_no_load blocks new KV loads and triggers fallback models or cold path to CPU.

Adaptive slice resizing feedback loop:
- Metrics to observe: kernel_utilization, per-SLA P50/P95/P99, KV_load_rate, per-stream stall_count.
- Controller (local to scheduler) runs an exponential moving average and adjusts slice size parameters every M seconds (default M=1s):
  - If P95 > target_p95_for_S0 => reduce high slice size by 20% and increase high weight (to favor more frequent draining)
  - If kernel_utilization < target_utilization_low => increase slice sizes up to max_tokens to improve throughput
  - If KV_load_rate rising faster than threshold and memory pressure high => bias towards slices that reuse hot keys and reduce prefetch of cold keys.
- Safety knobs: do not shrink slice below min_tokens and do not grow beyond max_tokens.

KV cache lifecycle and grace window heuristics:
- Each KV entry has an epoch_tag when loaded; scheduler maintains last_used_ts and reference_count estimates.
- Grace window (G) is a soft time during which scheduler will prioritize scheduling requests that reuse that epoch_tag. Default G=200ms.
- Eviction policy: prefer evicting low-reuse epoch_tags and cold keys; allow short reuse bursts across microbatches by delaying eviction for keys with reference_count>threshold.
- Diagnostic metric: kv_reuse_rate defined as fraction of prefetches that hit resident KV entries; target reuse_rate >= 0.65 for heavy workloads.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
- If prefetch cannot load required KV entries due to memory or credit limits, emit one of:
  - plan-B: use quantized CPU kernel as degraded path (higher latency but preserves correctness)
  - plan-C: use a smaller model variant pinned in memory for S0 requests (maintain low latency at cost of quality)
  - plan-D: respond with a short failure/ retry-after when backlog on high-priority streams exceeds emergency threshold
- Prefer plan-B for interactive streams if quality is still acceptable; prefer plan-C when plan-B would exceed latency SLOs.

Operational controls and knobs (configurable per deployment):
- target_utilization (float 0..1), min_tokens, max_tokens, kernel_timeslice_ms
- per-SLA base_by_SLA and weight_by_priority
- grace_window_ms and kv_memory_thresholds
- emergency_backlog_threshold and fallback_policy_map
- telemetry flags to emit per-slice diagnostics (slice_id, tps_bucket, kv_hint_keys, selected_decoder)

Experiments to run (short list):
1) Controlled replay: take production traces, simulate scheduler with TPS disabled vs enabled; measure SLO violations and throughput.
2) A/B: roll to a small fleet with high-priority interactive traffic; collect P50/P95/P99 and KV reuse rate.
3) Stress test: synthetic cold-KV storm to validate soft_no_load and fallback activation.
4) Tunable sweep: sweep target_utilization and observe tradeoff curve of cost-per-token vs P95 for S0 streams.

Open questions and risks:
- TPS calibration: weighting features (locality vs SLA) may be workload dependent. Need auto-calibration or conservative defaults.
- Complexity vs benefit: additional queues, slice formation, and handshake increases code paths. Aim for modular implementation behind a feature flag.
- Cross-node KV affinity: in multi-node serving, keeping KV hints colocated may conflict with load balancing; need policy to trade affinity vs even load.
- Fairness: ensure low-priority long-running requests don't starve; implement aging that boosts TPS slowly for requests waiting > X ms.

Implementation sketch (components):
- admission_worker: computes TPS and places request in queue
- scheduler: maintains rings, computes slice allocations, handles credit handshake
- decoder_adapter: lightweight stub exposing available_credits and soft_no_load signal
- kv_manager: tracks epochs, grace windows, and hot key sets
- controller: feedback loop for adaptive resizing

Minimal API changes (surface-level):
- Request metadata: add "affinity_key" and "estimated_max_tokens" optional fields to the public API
- Runtime signals internal: decoder.expose_credits(), decoder.soft_no_load(), scheduler.emit_slice(slice)

Example trace (walkthrough):
- T=0: three incoming requests: A(S0, est=12, affinity_key=k1), B(S2, est=200, affinity_key=null), C(S0, est=6, affinity_key=k1).
- TPS: A=80 (S0 base 60 + locality 20), B=10, C=85
- Scheduler sees available_credits=100 tokens. target_total_tokens=80. Weight allocation: high=40, mid=24, low=16.
- highQ contains A and C => slice_H = [A,C], total_tokens=18; hint_hot_keys={k1}
- midQ empty; lowQ contains B => slice_L=[B], total_tokens=200 but we cap to allocated low tokens; slice_L is split into two sub-slices (B1=16 tokens, B2=16 tokens) and remainder queued. Greedy co-placement places slice_H on decoder-3 with hot k1 resident. KV reuse hits reduce load.

Diagnostic logs to emit (per-slice): slice_id, priority_bucket, requests_count, total_tokens, hint_hot_keys, decoder_assigned, kv_loads_in_slice, latency_ms (end-to-end).

Next steps / action items:
- Prototype baseline scheduler implementing TPS->3 buckets and credit handshake. (Owner: Aisha, target prototype in 3 weeks)
- Add API telemetry for per-slice diagnostic logging (Owner: Marc)
- Run replay experiment on last 72h production trace; measure S0 P95 delta (Owner: Lena)

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally pragmatic: favor simple scoring and a small number of buckets to keep implementation complexity low. The key novelty is combining a credit handshake with a KV-aware grace window and adaptive slice resizing. Feedback welcome on the scoring formula and the grace-window sizing.
